# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
This comment does useful work in its first half and overreaches in its second. Sections 1–5 document real problems with the Halden paper, several of which I flagged in my review of it. The corrected estimates in Table 2 are a genuine contribution. But the headline conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact," isn't supported by the comment's own numbers, and it requires leaving out the Varden result that best meets the comment's own standards.

## What checks out

- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.8 → +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 → +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 → +10.8%.
- **Hours:** 34.6/40.3 → −14.1% and 34.8/40.4 → −13.9%.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 → −2.6%.
- **Conclusion:** the "four points" (3.8) and "six points" (20 − 13.9) are correct.
- **Attrition:** this is a genuine finding. The working paper said nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase," but seven left after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. Unless the microdata are wrong, the working paper misreported this, and the authors should correct it.

## 1. The abstract claims a correction the paper doesn't make

The abstract says "correcting the first three" problems reduces the gain to 10.8%. The first of those is attrition, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours. No row adjusts for the withdrawn organisations.

The abstract also lists revenue as one of four problems that "account for most of the reported gain." But the 23.4% figure never used revenue, so correcting revenue can't reduce it.

## 2. Attrition probably matters less than implied

The comment never estimates how much attrition matters, and a pessimistic bound suggests it's modest. Suppose all nine withdrawn organisations had an output index of 80, which is a per-hour gain of zero on scheduled hours. The organisation-weighted mean across all 70 would then be about (61 × 98.7 + 9 × 80) / 70 ≈ 96.3. That is still a gain of about 20% on scheduled hours.

Attrition is a real reporting failure, but it can't plausibly be "the organisations least able to cope" driving much of the 23.4%. A bounds analysis, or the first-month data for the seven that started, would settle this. The comment's own recommendation to analyse "all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw" applies here.

## 3. Table 2 mixes corrections with changes in sample

Each row uses a different subset (61, 23, 27, 17), and the weighting may differ too: row 1 is employee-weighted, and the others aren't stated. So the decline from +23.4% to +10.8% combines the effect of the corrections with differences between samples. Showing the uncorrected figure for each subset fixes this. For the 23, the manager index of 98.9 implies +23.6% on scheduled hours, so the like-for-like effect of record-based output is +23.6% → +18.9%. Do the same for the 17.

There are also no confidence intervals. With 17 organisations, the 10.8% figure is quite uncertain, and the comment holds others to a standard it doesn't meet itself.

## 4. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Starting from a scheduled 32 hours, "+0.7 hours per day" on four days plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives about 36.4 hours, not 34.6. The figures work if the 0.7 is per *week*: 32 + 0.3 (the baseline excess over 40) + 0.7 + 1.6 = 34.6. This is probably a typo, but it should be fixed.

## 5. "Record-based" output isn't automatically the truth

Table 1 treats submitted records as the benchmark, but some of those records are themselves biased. "Billable hours delivered" is an hours measure, so using it as output makes output per hour close to circular. When hours fall it falls too, by construction, even if the value delivered per hour went up, as with fixed-fee work. Tickets closed and units produced also miss changes in quality or complexity.

The 3.8-point gap is real evidence of manager optimism, since 19 of 23 managers rated higher than their records. But some of the gap may come from what the records leave out. Breaking the comparison down by type of record would show how much.

## 6. The novelty argument is testable with the data the authors already have

The pilot collected a monthly output index, and 27 organisations have continuous time-tracking. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should decline from month to month. The comment never checks this. Instead it extrapolates a straight line through two points of a self-reported energy measure that it doesn't link to output.

That extrapolation also gives month nine, not ten: the slope is (0.29 − 0.61)/3 ≈ −0.107 per month, which reaches zero around month 8.7.

"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" doesn't help the comment either. "Entirely an artifact" is also a positive claim that needs its own evidence.

## 7. Leaving out Varden's case-processing result

This is the most serious problem. The comment's recommended standard is record-based output, actual hours, and randomisation. Varden's case-processing stratum met all three and found +12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4).

That result can't be explained by measurement (output came from records, hours from timesheets) or selection (offices were randomised). Novelty is the only explanation left, and it ran nine months, longer than the Halden pilot. The comment cites Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature" and criticises its meetings analysis, but never mentions its main per-hour result. A conclusion that per-hour gains are "entirely" artifact has to address it.

A defensible conclusion would be something like: *Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated, and about 11% survives in a non-random subset. The best controlled evidence suggests real per-hour gains in queue-based work of roughly 10–15% over nine months, with durability unknown, and real output losses in presence-based work.*

## 8. The meetings section misdescribes what Varden did

- **"A subgroup selected after the results were known."** The seven offices were the treated arm of a stratum defined before randomisation. The calendar data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results existed. Only the decision to analyse it was unregistered.
- **"Should not be cited as a mechanism."** Varden didn't claim it was one. They said it "may account for part" of the gain, stressed that seven offices can't establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test.
- **What's missed.** The comment also overlooks the stronger half of the evidence. The difference in meeting time between arms (3.8 versus 7.1 hours) is a randomised contrast. The weak link is only the correlation between meeting cuts and output.

The caution is reasonable, but the criticism is aimed at claims Varden didn't make.

## 9. The data note contradicts the conclusion

The data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The abstract and conclusion then generalise to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. These need to be made consistent, and the data note is the one that's right.

## Smaller points

- **CPI as a deflator.** Many participants sell business services whose prices may not track consumer prices. Sector-specific deflators would be more accurate, though the direction of the correction is almost certainly right.
- **Revenue coverage.** "Revenue in participating organisations fell" applies only to the 52 that reported revenue.
- **Retail.** The 11.2% figure rests on three organisations, so it should be presented as illustrative.
- **Recommendations.** These are sound and closely match what Varden actually did.

## Overall

Sections 1–5 should stand, after fixing the hours typo, adding confidence intervals, and showing like-for-like subsets. Sections 6–8 and the abstract need rewriting to:
- test novelty directly with the monthly data,
- engage with Varden's case-processing result,
- describe the meetings analysis accurately, and
- replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion matching the evidence: the gain is overstated by roughly half, not zero, and it is sector-dependent.

I can draft a revised abstract and conclusion along those lines if useful.
